newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE-Murder on high seas sparks intrigue in Canada.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Murder on high seas sparks intrigue in Canada.

text.p: When four desperate Romanians spied the freighter Maersk Dubai docked in the Spanish port of Algeciras last March, they figured it was their ticket to a better life in a richer land.

Little did they know their fateful decision to stow away aboard the Canada-bound vessel would carry a death sentence for three of them and spark international intrigue involving four governments and countless lawyers.

Less than a day into their trans-Atlantic journey, two of the stowaways were found hiding in one of the ship's catwalks. The unwelcome guests, Radu Danciu and Petre Sangeorzan, were allegedly beaten and starved for days, then forced overboard by Taiwanese officers on a makeshift raft of oil drums and planks, according to eyewitnesses.

Before hitting the choppy waters below, one of the stowaways pleaded, begged and cried for mercy, a Filipino crew member of the Dubai told an extradition hearing in the eastern port city of Halifax, Nova Scotia. "He kissed my boots, my safety boots. He was begging in Spanish to help him beg to the captain that they will not be thrown into the water," Esmeraldo Esteban testified through an interpreter.

Another Filipino crewman, Ariel Boas, confirmed Esteban's story and said he saw a stowaway descend the ship's ladder into the water. "In my observation, he is very scared to go down," Boas told the court.

The barbarism resumed two months later when a third stowaway, Gheorghe Mihoc, was thrown into the mid-Atlantic, the witnesses told the court. One Romanian, Nicolae Pasca, survived the journey and is seeking asylum in Canada.

The twisted tale first came to the attention of Canadian authorities after eight Filipino crew members deserted the Dubai when it docked in Halifax. Acting on an international warrant, Royal Canadian Mounted Police stormed the boat, arrested six Taiwanese officers including the captain, and charged them with first-degree murder on behalf of Romania.

A seventh Taiwanese, the ship's radio officer, was arrested earlier when he jumped into the frigid waters of Halifax harbour. The accused denied any knowledge of the alleged crimes and Taiwanese government officials weighed in with a response based firmly in the unemotional world of legal semantics.

"We don't honestly care whether they have or have not committed these crimes," an official in Taipei's Economic and Cultural Office in Ottawa told Reuters. "These alleged criminal offences happened on the high seas, which gives us jurisdiction under international law. Canada has nothing to do with the case except that the ship is in its port."

When a crime is committed on the high seas, international law usually accords jurisdiction to the country under which the ship is flagged. Sometimes the home state of the accused is given jurisdiction. Either way, the men should be tried in Taiwan, said well-known Canadian criminal lawyer Edward Greenspan, who is representing the Taiwanese government.

Romania has proposed alternative travel plans. Bucharest insists that a 102-year-old extradition treaty with Canada gives it jurisdiction. That position is strengthened because Canada does not officially recognise Taiwan as a country.

China is also keeping a wary eye on the proceedings and has offered legal assistance to the accused, whom it considers Chinese citizens. Canada is the reluctant arbiter to this international tug-of-war. Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy has expressed frustration at the situation, saying it illustrates the need for an international criminal court.

Canadian police, however, are battling a more mundane problem: uncooperative witnesses. In the past two months, a curtain of silence has fallen upon the investigation as several of the Filipino witnesses have developed a case of legal jitters.

Rudolfo Miguel, considered by Canadian police to be the key witness to the murders, said a number of his relatives in the Phillipines had received death threats since he went ashore in Halifax with the story. He and two other Filipino seamen refused to testify until the federal government guaranteed their families safe passage to Canada.
Canadian authorities responded by charging the men with contempt of court. Only when faced with court sanctions were the three holdouts willing to testify.

Ironically, Canada is being asked to sort out an international mess that it may have helped create. Refugee workers suspect the ship's captain, Cheng Shiou, threw the stowaways overboard to avoid paying a fine of C$7,000 (US$5,090) per head imposed by Canada for illegal immigrants transported into the country.

"The fines create a financial incentive to do what the Taiwanese ship captain did," said Nancy Worsfold, spokeswoman for the Canadian Council for Refugees. She added that Canada was violating the basic right to asylum from persecution guaranteed in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

The Canadian government defends the fines. "It's an incentive to make ship companies responsible," Immigration Minister Lucienne Robillard said. But ultimately, it is Robillard's cabinet colleague, Justice Minister Allan Rock, who will close the book on Canada's role in the stowaway saga.

If the extradition hearing, still unfolding in a Halifax courtroom, determines that there is enough evidence for a murder trial, Rock will decide whether the accused travel east to the Orient or west to the Carpathians. Either way, the ship's officers will have to answer for crimes that one leading Romanian politician described as "cruelty, defying any moral law on the defence of life."
